# Where the extra words come from [5 min]{.time} {#extra-words}

::: notes
**Goal.** Everyone can explain why a vague prompt returns hedged, padded text in a different shape each time, and that the fix is in the prompt.

**Have ready.** Nothing live: the slides carry the examples.

**Clock.** 0:00 chat: what you delete first. 1:30 the two runs. 3:30 what you leave open. 5:00 time.

**Watch for.** The two runs heard as the output of a named product: keep the label, and never attribute them to a tool. "So the tool is bad": the lesson is the choices left open. Running long: this topic only frames the problem; the fix is the next topic.

**If asked.** Won't a better model fix this? I cannot speak for every model; whatever you leave open, the tool has to fill, and it fills it with the typical. Why does it hedge so much? Hedges and disclaimers are the typical wording for a clinical answer, so unless you say otherwise they come back. Can't I just say "be brief"? That is a start: length is one choice, and audience, structure and what to avoid matter too. Should I regenerate until it is right? That gives a different draft, not a better-specified one.

**Bridge.** "So what should you specify? Four things."
:::

## A vague prompt gets a vague answer {#vague-prompt}

::: {.lane}
[One line: "Write a progress note"]{.node .dark .grow} [→]{.op} [Left open: audience, length, structure, tone]{.node .ghost .grow} [→]{.op} [Filled with the typical]{.node .red .grow}
:::

[▲ Hedged, padded, and inconsistent in structure.]{.pointer}

::: {.fragment}
[The fix isn't a better model. It's a better prompt.]{.big .accent}
:::

::: {.move .chat}
[Chat · 1 min]{.tag} A wall of text comes back. What do you delete first? Type it.
:::

::: notes
**1:30.** Start with the chat: when a wall of text comes back, what do you delete first? Read out three answers; expect disclaimers and openers. Then the reason. Every choice you leave open, the audience, the length, the structure, the tone, the tool fills with the most typical pattern. The typical pattern for a clinical answer includes hedges, padding and a generic layout, so that is what comes back. Not because the tool is broken, but because the decisions were left to it. Then click for the line to remember: the fix is not a better model, it is a better prompt.

**Do.** Chat, one minute. Read out three answers, then click once. Nothing to paste on this slide.
:::

## Same vague prompt, two runs {#two-runs}

::: {.lane}
[Write a progress note for this patient. + the Case A facts underneath]{.node .dark .grow}
:::

::: {.fan}
[▼ Run 1]{.a} [▼ Run 2]{.a}
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.card}
[Run 1: prose]{.t}

[It is important to note that]{.accent} ... [may indicate]{.accent} ... [Please consult the treating physician.]{.accent}
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.card .teal}
[Run 2: headings]{.t}

Patient Summary. Key Findings. Considerations. Suggested Next Steps. Disclaimer.
:::
:::
:::

[▲ Left open: audience, length, structure, tone.]{.pointer}

[Illustrative: written for this course, not from a real tool]{.illustrative}

::: notes
**2:00.** Same vague prompt, the Case A facts underneath, two runs. Say twice that these are illustrative, written for this course, not captured from any tool and not a measurement. Run 1 is prose full of stock hedges, and it ends by telling the treating physician to consult the treating physician: the tool guessed the audience, and guessed wrong. Run 2 is headings ending in a disclaimer, and it turns the real plan on the card into "medication adjustment". Different shapes, because nothing said which. The words look careful and say nothing. A hedge is not a safety check; the real risk is the long, padded draft you skim, because skimming is how a changed dose gets through.

**Do.** No group step: these are not live runs. Ask aloud, no typing: which line would you delete first? Who chose the length? The structure? Nobody did.
:::

## What you leave open, the tool fills {#left-open}

| You left open | What tends to come back |
|-----------|-----------------------------|
| Audience | A general reader, not a colleague opening the chart |
| Length | A greeting, a restatement, a closing offer |
| Structure | A layout of its own, different on each run |
| Tone | Hedges and disclaimers standing in for judgment |

::: {.move .chat}
[Chat · 1 min]{.tag} The last thing you asked an assistant to write: which of these did you leave open? One sentence.
:::

::: notes
**1:30.** Every row is a choice the tool made because you did not. Audience: it writes for a general reader, not a colleague opening the chart. Length: a greeting, a restatement, a closing offer. Structure: a layout of its own, different on each run. Tone: hedges and disclaimers standing in for judgment. None of this is random, and most of it can be prevented before the tool writes anything. Lab One lets you see it on your own screen, so you do not have to take the table on trust. Close on the line: the fix is not a better model, it is a better prompt.

**Do.** Chat, 60 to 90 seconds. Read out two or three answers and match each to a row. Nobody needs to share what they typed into a tool.
:::

# Anatomy of a good prompt [10 min]{.time} {#anatomy}

::: notes
**Goal.** Everyone can name the four parts, say what each is for, and find the missing part in a weak prompt.

**Have ready.** Nothing live: the skeleton is on the slide, to paste into the chat. The demo comes in Module 3.

**Clock.** 0:00 the four parts. 2:00 the skeleton, saved. 4:00 which part is missing. 6:30 the answer. 7:45 the symptoms. 8:45 fix the prompt. 10:00 time.

**Watch for.** Role inflation ("You are a world-class..."): ask who the reader is. Real patient details creeping into FACTS: facts means a case card, not your patient. `[MISSING: what]` treated as a guarantee: it is not, you still read the output. Replying "no, shorter" in the same chat: fix the prompt instead.

**If asked.** Does the role really matter? It sets the register and the reader; it cannot supply a finding you did not give it. Do I need all four every time? For anything that reaches a chart, a colleague or a patient, yes; for a quick brainstorm less is fine, and the check still applies. Is this a lot of typing for one note? Write the skeleton once and save it; only the facts change. Whether it saves you time is yours to judge: Lab One part 1 puts two drafts side by side.

**Bridge.** "You have the framework. Now watch it work on a real note: same case, one prompt."
:::

## The four parts {#four-parts}

::: {.cards}
::: {.card}
[1]{.num}

[Role]{.t}

Who it is.

::: {.fragment}
A family physician, writing for a cardiologist.
:::
:::
::: {.card .teal}
[2]{.num}

[Context]{.t}

What it knows.

::: {.fragment}
Only the facts you give it.
:::
:::
::: {.card}
[3]{.num}

[Format]{.t}

What shape to return.

::: {.fragment}
"Maximum 150 words", not "short".
:::
:::
::: {.card .teal}
[4]{.num}

[Constraints]{.t}

What to avoid.

::: {.fragment}
"Do not add doses", not "be accurate".
:::
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.fan}
[▼]{.a} [▼]{.a} [▼]{.a} [▼]{.a}
:::

::: {.lane .sm}
[One prompt: nothing left for the tool to guess]{.node .out .grow}
:::

[Who it is, what it knows, what shape to return, what to avoid.]{.accent}
:::

::: notes
**2:00.** The last topic showed what vagueness costs. The fix is four decisions, made on purpose, in the same order every time, on any prompt, not only notes. Click through one part at a time. Role: who it writes as, and for whom; it sets the register, not the facts, so "a world-class cardiologist" adds no knowledge. Context: the facts it may use and what the output is for, only those. Format: the exact shape; "short" is a wish, "maximum 150 words" a limit you can check. Constraints: name the forbidden thing; "do not add doses" works, "be accurate" does not. Common mistakes: a flattering role and no audience, no "use only these", adjectives for length, constraints written as hopes. Last click: say the memory line.

**Do.** Click once per part, then once more. No activity here; watch the chat for questions.
:::

## The skeleton: copy it and save it {#skeleton}

::: {.lane .sm}
[Role]{.node} [Context]{.node .teal} [Facts: the slot]{.node .same} [Format]{.node} [Constraints]{.node .teal}
:::

[▲ FACTS is not a fifth part. It is the slot under CONTEXT where your facts go.]{.pointer}

::: {.paste-long style="font-size:1.5em"}
{{< include _paste-four-part-skeleton.md >}}
:::

[▲ Copy prompt on your slide. Paste it into a note on your device.]{.pointer}

::: {.move .solo}
[Solo · 1 min]{.tag} Save it as "four-part skeleton". Lab One uses it.
:::

::: notes
**2:00.** This is the skeleton, and you copy it now. FACTS is not a fifth part: it is the slot under Context where your facts go. The line to memorize is in Context: use only the facts below, and if something needed is missing, write MISSING and say what, instead of guessing. That turns a silent invention into a visible gap you can see and fill. It is not a guarantee, so you still read the output. Point back at the memory line: who it is, what it knows, what shape to return, what to avoid.

**Do.** Tell them to click Copy prompt on their slide, and paste the block into the chat too. Everyone saves it in a note on their device; Lab One part 1 uses it. Solo, one minute. No assistant needed for this step.
:::

Nobody has to argue with an output: the prompt itself shows what is wrong, and the next slide gives the answers.

## What each prompt left out {#gap-answer}

::: {.lane .sm .fragment}
[Prompt 1]{.node .dark} [Role]{.node} [Context]{.node .teal} [Format: missing]{.node .ghost} [Constraints]{.node .teal}
:::

::: {.lane .sm .fragment}
[Prompt 2]{.node .dark} [Role]{.node} [Context]{.node .teal} [Format]{.node} [Constraints: missing]{.node .ghost}
:::

::: {.lane .sm .fragment}
[Prompt 3]{.node .dark} [Role]{.node} [Context and facts: missing]{.node .ghost} [Format]{.node} [Constraints]{.node .teal}
:::

[▲ The dashed box is the part that prompt left to the tool. Nobody had to argue with an output.]{.pointer}

::: notes
**1:15.** Reveal one at a time and ask for each: what would you see in the output? Prompt 1 has no Format, so layout and length are left to the tool and the shape drifts from run to run. Prompt 2 has no Constraints: expect hedges, unrequested advice and drifting units. Prompt 3 has no Context and no facts: the tool has nothing to work from, so whatever it writes is filled in, not drawn from your patient. The prompt showed what was wrong.

**Do.** Click once per answer. Take each "what would you see" from the chat, then confirm it on the next slide.
:::

## Every missing part leaves a mark {#symptoms}

::: {.cards}
::: {.card .red}
[Missing: Role]{.t}

Wrong reader: a chart note that talks to the patient, a letter that reads like a textbook.
:::
::: {.card .red}
[Missing: Context]{.t}

Details you never gave it, or generic filler where your facts belong.
:::
::: {.card .red}
[Missing: Format]{.t}

A different layout on every run, and a length you did not choose.
:::
::: {.card .red}
[Missing: Constraints]{.t}

Hedges, disclaimers, unrequested advice, units that drift.
:::
:::

[▲ Read the symptom, then name the missing part.]{.pointer}

::: notes
**1:00.** When an answer goes wrong, read these from the symptom. A chart note that talks to the patient, or a letter that reads like a textbook: no Role. Details you never gave it: no Context. A new layout every run: no Format. Hedges and drifting units: no Constraints. The symptom tells you which decision was left to the tool.

**Do.** No activity. If someone names a symptom from their own use, match it to a card.
:::

## Fix the prompt, not the answer {#fix-the-prompt}

::: {.flow}
::: {.step}
[1]{.num} Find the symptom
:::
::: {.step}
[2]{.num} Name the missing part
:::
::: {.step}
[3]{.num} Fix the prompt
:::
::: {.step}
[4]{.num} Run it again in a fresh chat
:::
:::

::: {.cards}
::: {.card .dashed}
[Not this]{.t}

Replying "no, shorter" in the same chat.
:::
::: {.card .teal}
[This]{.t}

Save the version that works. Your list can start from the course's prompt library.
:::
:::

::: notes
**1:15.** When an answer is wrong, resist replying "no, shorter" in the same chat. Find the symptom, name the missing part, fix the prompt, and run it again in a fresh chat. A prompt you have fixed once is a prompt you can keep, so save the ones that work. The course's prompt library holds every reusable prompt from today, and your own list can grow from it.

**Do.** No activity. The links go into the chat at the end of the call.
:::

# Structure fixes it (notes) [5 min]{.time} {#structure-notes}

::: notes
**Goal.** Everyone can see the one-line template prompt as the four parts squeezed into a line, and can run three passes on a drafted note.

**Have ready.** Your own assistant on a new chat, to run the SOAP prompt as the group does. The handout's illustrative note is your fallback if a tool misbehaves.

**Clock.** 0:00 the one line against the template. 1:30 run the SOAP prompt. 3:00 three passes, and the chat. 5:00 time.

**Watch for.** The A line: a tool is most tempted to add a diagnosis there, so read it against the facts. A draft read as what every tool returns: the handout's illustrative note was written for this course, and your own run is one run. Walking the prompt line by line: this is five minutes, so point at the four labels and move on.

**If asked.** Can I just use the one-line version? For a quick draft, yes; the full prompt adds the role and the only-these-facts line, which is the documentation-safety part. Does it obey the 150-word limit? Count; a limit is a request, not a lock, and if it dropped a fact to fit, raise the limit. My hospital uses a different note format: replace the FORMAT line with your template and change nothing else. Will this save me time? Lab One part 1 puts two drafts side by side so you can judge; there is no number from us.

**Bridge.** "Same skeleton, different fills. Next: a referral letter, a discharge summary and a handout, three cases, fifteen minutes."
:::

## Structure fixes it {#structure-fix}

::: {.lane}
[Case A facts]{.node .same .fixed} [+]{.op} [One line: "Write a progress note for this patient."]{.node .change .grow} [→]{.op} [Long, hedged, a new shape each run]{.node .red .fixed}
:::

::: {.lane}
[Case A facts]{.node .same .fixed} [+]{.op} [A template: SOAP note, exact format, under 150 words, no hedging]{.node .change .grow} [→]{.op} [One fixed structure]{.node .out .fixed}
:::

[▲ The four parts, squeezed into one line: a format, a length, a constraint.]{.pointer}

::: notes
**1:30.** Back to the vague prompt from the start of the module, now as one application of the framework. Top: write a progress note for this patient; it tends to come back long, hedged and shaped differently each time. Bottom: write a SOAP note in this exact format, under 150 words, no hedging language. That is the four parts squeezed into one line: a format, a length and a constraint. Spread out, with a role and an only-these-facts context, it is the full Case A prompt on the next slide. Point at the four labels, then stop. Lab One shows you the difference.

**Do.** No group step. Click on; do not read the prompt line by line.
:::

## Three passes before it goes near a chart {#three-passes}

::: {.cards}
::: {.card}
[1]{.num}

[Numbers]{.t}

[]{.chk} Every value and unit against the facts.
:::
::: {.card .teal}
[2]{.num}

[Medicines]{.t}

[]{.chk} Name, dose, frequency, new or continued.
:::
::: {.card}
[3]{.num}

[Plan]{.t}

[]{.chk} Every item present, none added.
:::
:::

[▲ Run all three on your own draft. Lab One, part 1, puts them on a clock.]{.pointer}

::: {.move .chat}
[Chat · 1 min]{.tag} In your note: which medicine is new, and how many plan items are there? Type both.
:::

::: notes
**2:00.** Three short passes, the same every time, on your own draft. Numbers: every value and unit against the source. Medicines: name, dose, frequency, new or continued. Plan: every item present, none added; read the A line with it, because that is where a tool is most tempted to add a diagnosis you did not make. These passes are where "invented, omitted, altered" show up in a note. On Case A, amlodipine stays at 5 mg and losartan 50 mg is new; the plan has six items. Count the words too: a limit is a request, not a lock; if a fact was dropped to fit, raise the limit.

**Do.** Chat, 60 seconds. Read out two answers. Tick your own draft on the shared screen as the group ticks theirs.
:::

# Same framework, three more jobs [15 min]{.time} {#three-more-jobs}

::: notes
**Goal.** Everyone can see one skeleton produce three different documents, name the hot spot to check in each, and say who supplies the numbers and the red flags.

**Have ready.** Your own assistant, to run each prompt as the group does; the handout's illustrative outputs are your fallback if a tool misbehaves. Never read a prompt aloud.

**Clock.** 0:00 the three jobs. 1:15 referral, run and check. 4:15 discharge summary, run and check. 7:30 handout, run and check. 9:45 the gap. 11:15 Arabic (optional). 12:00 your constraint. 15:00 time.

**Watch for.** Time: fifteen minutes becomes twenty, so give each document about three minutes. "Just this once, let it write the red flags": hold the line, kindly. Drift into Day Two's demo: today is three cases and one skeleton, not one event in three audiences. Any comment on how good a tool is at Arabic: say only that a fluent reader checks it. Real cases offered as examples: redirect to the card.

**If asked.** Can the tool write the red flags if I ask? It can produce a list, but a red flag the tool wrote is a clinical decision you did not make; write your own, put them in FACTS, and let the tool word them. Why copy the medicine list exactly? The next doctor acts on it, and a tool tidying a list can merge lines, round a dose or shorten a duration, all fluently. Can I use this on my own patient? The framework, yes; the identifiers, no. No patient identifiers into a consumer AI tool. Ever. Full stop.

**Bridge.** "One method, four documents. Now, which tool do you put it in? Not all AI is the same."
:::

## One skeleton, three jobs {#three-jobs}

::: {.lane .sm}
[Case C facts]{.node .same .grow} [→]{.op} [Referral letter, for a cardiologist]{.node .grow} [→]{.op} [Question first. 200 words at most.]{.node .out .grow} [→]{.op} [The allergy must appear]{.node .red .grow}
:::

::: {.lane .sm}
[Case B facts]{.node .same .grow} [→]{.op} [Discharge summary, for the family doctor]{.node .grow} [→]{.op} [Five fixed headings. 250 words at most.]{.node .out .grow} [→]{.op} [Medicines copied exactly as listed]{.node .red .grow}
:::

::: {.lane .sm}
[Case D facts]{.node .same .grow} [→]{.op} [Patient handout, for the baby's parents]{.node .grow} [→]{.op} [Short headings, plain words. 200 words at most.]{.node .out .grow} [→]{.op} [No warning signs or doses you did not give]{.node .red .grow}
:::

[▲ Left to right: the facts, the job and its reader, the format, the one constraint that matters most.]{.pointer}

::: notes
**1:15.** The skeleton does not change. Four things do: the reader, the format, the constraint that matters most, and what you check afterward. Three documents you write every week, each with its own case inside the prompt. A referral for a cardiologist who has not met the patient: the allergy must appear. A discharge summary for the family doctor taking over: the medicines copied exactly as listed. A handout for a baby's parents: no warning signs and no doses you did not give. Day Two turns this around, one case for three audiences. Today it is three cases and one skeleton.

**Do.** No group step. Trace one lane aloud: the facts, the job and its reader, the format, the one constraint that matters most.
:::

::: {.card .teal}
[Against the facts you pasted, tick each one]{.t}

[]{.chk} The question is in paragraph 1, and the tool has not answered it

[]{.chk} The allergy: penicillin (rash), not upgraded

[]{.chk} Pulse about 108 and ECG rate 112, neither replaced the other

[]{.chk} Not done yet: echocardiogram, anticoagulation
:::

[▲ A tick if it matches. If not, write altered or omitted.]{.pointer}

:::

::: notes
**1:45.** Check your letter against the four ticks. The question is in paragraph one, worded as asked, and the tool has not answered it. The allergy is present and still penicillin (rash): not dropped, not upgraded. The two heart rates are two measurements, pulse about 108 on exam and ventricular rate 112 on the ECG; neither may replace the other. What is not done, no echocardiogram and no anticoagulation, is stated. In the handout's illustrative letter the allergy sits in the last paragraph.

**Do.** Tick your own letter on the shared screen as the group ticks theirs. Chat, one minute. Read out two answers.

**1:15.** The reader is the doctor who takes over, often days later and without the chart open, so the format is five fixed headings, and one rule the tool must not bend: the discharge medicines are copied exactly as listed. This is the job where altered costs the most, because the next doctor acts on it. Case B, a fictional patient, is inside the prompt; the first line gives the diagnosis. ## Check the discharge summary {#discharge-check}

::: {.card .teal}
[Against the facts you pasted, tick each one]{.t}

[]{.chk} Medicines copied exactly: name, dose, frequency, duration

[]{.chk} "3 more days at home" and the 7-day total, not merged

[]{.chk} Both cultures pending, none turned "negative"

[]{.chk} Chest imaging at 6 weeks "only if symptoms persist"

[]{.chk} Vaccination: not documented, not "up to date"
:::

[▲ Safest habit: delete the tool's medicine list and paste in the real one.]{.pointer}

::: {.move .chat}
[Chat · 1 min]{.tag} Which two results are still pending in your summary? Type them.
:::

::: notes
**2:00.** Case B: five fixed headings, and the medicines copied exactly, because altered costs the most here. Read the medicine list line by line; check that 3 more days at home and the 7-day total were not merged. Pending means pending: no growth at 48 h with a final result pending is never negative. The two pending are the blood cultures' final result and the sputum culture. Follow-up keeps "only if symptoms persist", and all five reasons to return sooner are there. A tool tidying a list can merge two lines, round a dose or shorten a duration, and each reads fluently. Safest habit: delete the tool's medicine list and paste in the real one.

**Do.** Tick your own summary on the shared screen. Chat, one minute: everyone types the two pending results. Read out two, then point at the medicine lines.
:::

**1:15.** Now the reader is a worried parent, not a colleague: short sentences, plain words, no jargon, and only the diagnosis, the home plan and when to return. Case D lists no warning signs beyond "sooner if worse", so the prompt tells the tool to leave a gap rather than write its own. Case D, a fictional baby, is inside the prompt. New chat, paste it, first draft only.

**Do.** Tell them to click Copy prompt on their slide, and paste the block into the chat too. Run it on your screen as the group runs it on theirs. Anyone whose assistant misbehaves follows your screen.
:::

::: notes
**1:00.** Check your handout against the four ticks. Warning signs: only yours; if one appears that you did not supply, delete it, because a red flag the tool wrote is a clinical decision you did not make. Medicines and doses: none added, and "no antibiotics" and "no bronchodilators" are still negatives. Timing: "24 to 48 hours" and "sooner if worse" unchanged, with no recovery time added. The explanation of the illness is the tool's general knowledge, not your facts: read it as you would a colleague's.

**Do.** Solo, one minute. Tick your own handout on the shared screen as the group ticks theirs.
:::

## The gap is the point {#you-supply}

::: {.card .teal}
[Under "When to come back", the tool wrote]{.t}

`[MISSING: warning signs the parents should watch for]`
:::

[Illustrative, written for this course]{.illustrative}

[No warning signs in the facts]{.node .ghost .grow} [→]{.op} [The tool leaves a visible gap]{.node .out .grow} [→]{.op} [You write the red flags]{.node .change .grow}
:::

[You supply the numbers and the red flags.]{.big}

[The tool only words them.]{.big .accent}

::: {.move .chat}
[Chat · 30 sec]{.tag} Case D lists no warning signs. Who decides what goes under "When to come back"? One word.
:::

::: notes
**1:30.** Case D lists no warning signs beyond "sooner if worse", so the prompt tells the tool to leave a gap rather than write its own. If your handout shows this line, the tool did what you asked, and the gap is the point of this module. Filling it is your clinical judgment: write the signs you would tell this family, add them to FACTS, and run it again. A red flag the tool wrote is a clinical decision you did not make; the same goes for doses and durations in a discharge summary. You supply the numbers and the red flags. The tool only words them.

**Do.** Chat, 30 seconds. Read out a few answers. Do not collect red flags from the group.
:::

## Arabic output: a fluent reader checks it {#arabic-check}

Case D: the mother prefers written instructions in Arabic.

::: {.card .tint}
[A fluent Arabic reader must check the Arabic before it reaches a family.]{.big}
:::

{{< include _paste-m2-arabic-language-line.md >}}

[▲ Copy prompt on your slide. An optional line for the end of the handout prompt.]{.pointer}

Question 3: Would I catch it if it were wrong?

::: {.move .solo}
[Solo · optional]{.tag} Try it only if you read Arabic well enough to check it.
:::

::: notes
**0:45.** Optional: use it if the group reads Arabic or someone asks; otherwise skip it and give the time to the last slide. Case D says the mother prefers written instructions in Arabic, so one added line asks for the handout in simple everyday Arabic, with the English underneath. The English lets you compare, but it does not replace a fluent reader. A fluent Arabic reader must check the Arabic before it reaches a family. If you cannot read the Arabic yourself, question three is a no, and that is the signal to slow down, not the finding to accept. I make no claim about how well any tool writes Arabic: ask a colleague, or do not send it.

**Do.** Tell them to click Copy prompt on their slide, and paste the block into the chat too. Say the check aloud. Only those who read Arabic run it; the rest follow your screen.
:::
